summary:
Santa Fe province has no trans-specific statute of its own that the source inventory documents. For a trans visitor, the operative legal picture is Argentina's national framework, which extends to every province. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and has allowed an 'X' marker on the national identity document since 2021.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive decree. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei published DNU 62/2025, amending Article 11 of the 2012 Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, alongside DNU 61/2025, which alters prison-sentencing law to change the placement of transgender detainees. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations interviewed by Agencia Presentes called both measures unconstitutional and said the abrupt suspension of adolescent treatments endangers transgender youth; both decrees face judicial challenge and apply to every province.

Enforcement exposure in 2025 was severe. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours. Cases in which security-force personnel were the perpetrators rose from 17 to 64, a doubling that materially changes what a trans visitor should expect from police contact.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, described a chaotic and desperate situation under the Milei government. They reported that the national Women/Gender/Diversity Ministry was eliminated, that trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law covering 1 per cent of public-sector posts were dismissed, and that the quota is no longer being implemented. They also reported that the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Santa Fe is nonetheless better documented than most provinces on the violence question: the provincial government publishes violent-death statistics that include transfemicidios and travesticidios, and national registers name provincial transfemicide victims. No provincial enforcement series with a source was found in the inventory.

On judicial protection for gender-motivated killing, Argentina's Supreme Court in April 2025 left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases.
tangentialFactors:
The deterioration is measurable at the level of institutional machinery as well as violence. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, for gender recognition, and for the registration of civil-society organisations — an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

The 2025 hate-crime record coincides with documented policy hostility at the national level: the elimination of the gender ministry, the non-implementation of the federal trans employment quota, and the February 2025 decrees. Activists interviewed in April 2025 linked these measures to a rise in community vulnerability.

The national marriage-equality position, legalised in 2010 as the first in Latin America, is unchanged and not implicated in the decrees; the practical exposure for a trans visitor runs through the decrees, police contact, and the absence of applied hate-motivation aggravation.

Santa Fe's practice of publishing transfemicidio and travesticidio figures is unusual among Argentine provinces and makes local anti-trans violence more visible there than elsewhere; it does not by itself indicate a lower rate.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents of Santa Fe live under the national Legal Gender Recognition Law 26.743, which has applied in the province since 2012, but the February 2025 decrees restricting adolescent transition-related care and altering prison placement for transgender detainees apply here as they do nationwide.

The provincial government publishes violent-death statistics that count transfemicidios and travesticidios among causes of death, and national registers identify transfemicide victims from Santa Fe, giving residents and advocacy groups a provincial evidence base that most provinces lack.

Employment access for transgender residents is affected by the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which activists report is no longer being implemented under the current national government, and by the elimination of the national Women/Gender/Diversity Ministry.

The 'X' marker available on the national identity document since 2021 remains available to residents, and the right to legal gender change without medical intervention remains formally in force, though activists describe enforcement of the 2012 law as no longer guaranteed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Santa Fe provincial statute on gender identity, hate crime, facilities access or prison placement was located in the source inventory; the inventory's finding that no such provincial series exists with a source is recorded as unresolved rather than as an absence of law.

The inventory does not report enforcement figures for the two February 2025 decrees in Santa Fe, nor whether the judicial challenges to DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025 have been resolved in provincial courts; both remain open questions.

Whether the 'X' DNI marker is accepted on Santa Fe provincial documents, and what provincial facilities and healthcare protocols apply to transgender visitors, are not sourced and are not stated.

The inventory does not separate trans-specific hate crimes from the 2025 total of 227, although Agencia Presentes describes trans women as bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.
